top_choice_rationale: P002 rewards one identifiable discovery, the Kiyotaki-Moore collateral-constraint mechanism. A durable, pledgeable asset ties credit limits to asset prices, so small shocks become persistent downturns. It has about three decades of extension and use, including the 2007-09 crisis, so maturity is not in doubt. The two-name attribution is the cleanest on the slate and needs no arbitrary cut under the three-name cap. The citation is deliberately narrow: it does not claim the Bernanke-Gertler accelerator or the intermediary-finance strand. The main cost is marginal novelty after the 2022 prize and the indirect or calibrated aggregate evidence. I judge the mechanism distinct from bank runs and intermediation. P004 is second because its foundational importance is high but a three-name cut of an eight-name field is hard to defend. P001 is third because its measurement and exposure designs are strong but too recent to have been tested over time. P003 is fourth because it is mature and concentrated in credit but has weaker cross-country identification. A prize in any of the four is preferred to no award.
recusal_note: Disclosures only, none adjudicated. Per Krusell (secretary, frequent co-author, IIES colleague) is the sole explicit supporter of P004, my second choice. I co-authored with Timo Boppart and Richard Friberg, who support P001. My social-mobility research is adjacent to P001. My profile shows no co-authorship or institutional tie to Kiyotaki, Moore, Gertler or Gilchrist (P002), or to the credited names in P003 and P004 beyond those disclosed. My 2018 presentation speech and the 2018 Scientific Background citing my work concern climate economics, not a candidate on this slate.
